title: Neural network inverse design of nanophotonic scintillators
authors: Nathan Regev, Avner Shultzman, Francis Loignon-Houle, Charles Roques-Carmes, Ido Kaminer
abstract: Scintillators are materials converting high-energy radiation into optical light, essential in a range of technologies such as medical imaging systems and security scanners. Scintillator development and optimization have remained limited by the complexity of their underlying physics, involving stochastic cascades of electron-electron, electron-phonon, and electron-photon interactions. Such processes are typically modeled by non-differentiable Monte Carlo simulations, limiting the applicability of machine learning for scintillator development. Here we present a physics-informed neural network that learns the scintillation cascade process from the incident high-energy particle to photon emission, substantially accelerating scintillator design and optimization. Combining this neural network with photonic simulations enables end-to-end differentiable optimization of the scintillator geometry. This allows us to optimize for arbitrary figures of merit, such as specific target emission patterns.. We demonstrate the concept and characterize it relative to previous approaches by inverse design of nanophotonic scintillators for X-ray imaging.
summary: The paper introduces a Physics-Informed Neural Network (SPINN) framework to overcome the computational bottleneck in designing scintillators. By replacing slow, non-differentiable Monte Carlo simulations with a differentiable neural network surrogate, it enables efficient gradient-based inverse design optimization for novel nanophotonic structures. This breakthrough accelerates materials discovery by linking structure geometry directly to desired optical performance.
main_problem: Scintillator development is limited by complex, stochastic physics modeled by non-differentiable Monte Carlo simulations, preventing efficient machine learning optimization.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated an end-to-end differentiable inverse design framework for nanophotonic scintillators using a Physics-Informed Neural Network (SPINN).
method: They replaced computationally expensive and non-differentiable Monte Carlo simulations with PINN surrogate models to learn the relationship between structure geometry and light emission.
model_or_system: The system is a nanophotonic scintillator, often implemented as multilayer stacks. The model involves coupling the SPINN (surrogate for electron cascade) with a differentiable photonic simulator to optimize structural parameters.
key_observables: Far-field signal intensity distribution, total light yield ($L(\vec{d})$), and spatial photon emission profiles ($ho(z, r)$).
important_parameters: Layer thicknesses (nanoscale dimensions), refractive indices, X-ray energy (e.g., 8 keV), and the number of latent parameters ($K$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that a PINN can accurately surrogate the complex physics, though comparisons showed that explicit physical constraints (Prior Layer Model) outperformed purely data-driven autoencoders.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the optimization flow using SPINN, comparing the predicted signal from different models (Autoencoder vs. Prior Layer Model vs. Exponential Model) against Monte Carlo ground truth across varying sample thicknesses.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first identifying the modeling gap (MC limitations), proposing the PINN surrogate framework, detailing the training methodology using self-supervised learning on simulated data, and finally validating the approach through inverse design optimization for specific scintillators.
why_interesting: This work represents a powerful application of ML to solve complex physical simulation bottlenecks. The use of PINNs to bridge stochastic physics (electron transport) with deterministic optics is highly relevant for modeling open quantum systems where full time-evolution simulations are intractable.
